name: Hard-easy effect
statement: Confidence exceeds accuracy on hard sets of questions and falls short of it on easy ones, and little of the pattern is left once two measurement artefacts are removed.
meaning: The paradigm is a two-alternative general knowledge question answered with a confidence report on a scale from .5 to 1.0. Over/underconfidence is defined as mean confidence minus proportion correct. Plot that score against proportion correct across studies and the line slopes down. Lichtenstein and Fischhoff put the crossing point near a proportion correct of .75, as Juslin, Winman and Olsson report them. Judges look overconfident on hard item sets and underconfident on easy ones. The psychological reading is that confidence tracks difficulty too weakly. The statistical reading is that proportion correct sits on both axes, so the two quantities move against each other whatever the judges are doing.

origin.note: Their paper is titled "Do those who know more also know more about how much they know?". It was not obtained. Elsevier keeps it closed, and on 21 September 2026 Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all recorded no open copy. The Internet Archive holds no item for it, and DTIC answered a plain request with a block and a browser-like one with a maintenance page. Its finding is reported here from Juslin, Winman and Olsson. They write that Lichtenstein and Fischhoff found overconfidence for item sets with a proportion correct below about .75, and underconfidence above it. The same effect travels as the difficulty effect, after Griffin and Tversky, and as the discriminability effect, after Ferrell and McGoey.

evidence: Juslin, Winman and Olsson assembled the data available to them in June 1998 from studies using two-alternative general knowledge items and the half-range confidence scale. They had 95 independent data points from selected item samples and 35 from representative samples, where items were drawn at random from a defined natural environment. Mean confidence was .73 under both methods, with 95% confidence intervals of plus or minus .01 and .02. Proportion correct was .64 for selected samples and .72 for representative ones. Over/underconfidence was .09 for selected samples and .01 for representative ones, each with a 95% interval of plus or minus .02. Regressing over/underconfidence on proportion correct gave a slope of -.72 for the selected samples, with proportion correct accounting for 70% of the variance, and -.53 for the representative samples, accounting for 58%. That downward slope is the hard-easy effect, and it appears under both methods of choosing items.

replication.headline: The pattern in raw data is not in dispute, and correcting for both artefacts leaves a slope that is not reliably different from zero.
replication.detail: Juslin, Winman and Olsson name three mechanisms that produce the slope without any judge being biased. The confidence scale ends at .5 and 1.0, so response error near the ends can push in only one direction. Proportion correct appears in both the predictor and the outcome, which they call linear dependency and which forces a negative correlation by itself. Confidence and accuracy are only correlated, so each regresses on the other, a line of argument they trace to Erev, Wallsten and Budescu. They corrected the 17 representative samples collected in their own laboratory. Uncorrected, the slope was -.63, 95% CI plus or minus .31, with proportion correct accounting for 51% of the variance. Correcting for scale-end effects alone left -.41 and 31%. Correcting for linear dependency alone left -.42 and 23%, using Klayman, Soll, González-Vallejo and Barlas's method of splitting each sample into a definition set and a measurement set. Correcting for both left a slope of -.20, 95% CI plus or minus .27, with proportion correct accounting for 6% of the variance. They mark that slope as non-significant and call what survives the remains of the hard-easy effect. The corrected model predicts overconfidence of .03 at a proportion correct of .5 and underconfidence of .06 at a proportion correct of 1.0. Juslin and colleagues report that Klayman and colleagues, applying the same correction across eight topics of general knowledge items, also found no reliable hard-easy effect remaining. Merkle later derived necessary and sufficient conditions for observing the effect. He concluded that judges show it in almost all realistic situations. That includes judges perfectly calibrated at the item level, and judges whose confidence is unrelated to the questions. On his account the pattern is real and tells a researcher nothing about how confidence is produced.

study.cite: Juslin, P., Winman, A., & Olsson, H. (2000). Naive empiricism and dogmatism in confidence research: A critical examination of the hard-easy effect. Psychological Review, 107(2), 384-396.

limits: Everything above concerns two-alternative general knowledge items scored on the half-range scale, which is one paradigm. Juslin, Winman and Olsson argue that scale-end effects, linear dependency and regression apply across judgement research, and their review does not test that. Their corrections were applied to 17 samples from a single laboratory, doubled to 34 points by swapping the roles of the definition and measurement sets. They warn that the corrections are stacked on top of each other and that each carries assumptions. Merkle's derivation rests on a response-error model with a variance of .03 and on true probabilities drawn from a beta distribution, and he states that a beta distribution cannot generally produce multimodal cases. Lichtenstein and Fischhoff's 1977 paper, Klayman and colleagues' 1999 paper and Erev, Wallsten and Budescu's 1994 paper were not obtained, so what they found is quoted here from Juslin, Winman and Olsson rather than read. The artefact case has been argued against in print, in the same journal and year. Brenner holds that splitting observed miscalibration into true and artefactual parts is unsound, because neither the true judgment nor the error term is defined. Wallsten, Erev and Budescu reply that models are needed to read data at all, and concede only that the two constructs are badly named. Their reply was read as an abstract, not in full. On 21 September 2026 this entry searched Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex and the open web for a reanalysis that controls scale-end effects and linear dependency and still recovers the effect. Later work naming the effect exists, in education, radiology and decision analysis, but no such reanalysis of the confidence corpus was found.
misreadings: The effect is not a property of a judge. Merkle shows that both perfectly calibrated judges and judges whose confidence is unrelated to the stimulus produce it, so its presence cannot separate good judges from bad ones. Nor does it show that people cannot tell a hard test from an easy one. Merkle reports that Gigerenzer, Hoffrage and Kleinbölting found judges fairly accurate when asked outright how many questions they had got right. The inaccuracy shows up only when accuracy is inferred from item-by-item confidence. A single pair of tests settles nothing in either direction, and Merkle notes that Gigerenzer and colleagues discussed two studies yielding four apparent reversals of the effect, which the covariance that defines it can absorb. The effect has also been used as an argument rather than a finding. Griffin and Tversky held that the difficulty effect explained away Gigerenzer and colleagues' result that representative item sampling removes overconfidence. Juslin, Winman and Olsson matched hard samples on difficulty, both sets at a proportion correct of .65. Over/underconfidence was .10 for 29 selected samples and .05 for 12 representative ones, so difficulty does not account for the gap.

sources.text: Lichtenstein, S., & Fischhoff, B. (1977). Do those who know more also know more about how much they know? Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 20(2), 159-183. Not obtained. On 21 September 2026 Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar each recorded the article as closed, the Internet Archive held no item for it, and DTIC answered a plain request with a block and a browser-like one with a maintenance page. Its finding is quoted on this page from Juslin, Winman and Olsson, who state it in their introduction.

Juslin, P., Winman, A., & Olsson, H. (2000). Naive empiricism and dogmatism in confidence research: A critical examination of the hard-easy effect. Psychological Review, 107(2), 384-396. Read in full as the published article, from a copy on Andreas Ortmann's course page at CERGE-EI. Every figure on this page that is not credited elsewhere was checked against its text and its Tables 3 and 4.

Merkle, E. C. (2009). The disutility of the hard-easy effect in choice confidence. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 16(1), 204-213. Read in full as the published article. The PDF came from rd.springer.com on 21 September 2026.

Klayman, J., Soll, J. B., González-Vallejo, C., & Barlas, S. (1999). Overconfidence: It depends on how, what, and whom you ask. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 79(3), 216-247. Not obtained. ScienceDirect, Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all recorded it as closed on 21 September 2026, and no repository or faculty copy answered. Only the abstract was read, at PubMed. What this page says they found is quoted from Juslin, Winman and Olsson. Their own abstract adds that overconfidence persists for subjective confidence intervals, which is a different measure from the one this page covers.

Erev, I., Wallsten, T. S., & Budescu, D. V. (1994). Simultaneous over- and underconfidence: The role of error in judgment processes. Psychological Review, 101(3), 519-527. Not obtained. Unpaywall records no open location, PsycNet answers with a purchase page, the Wayback Machine holds no capture of that file, and the Technion repository record carries no file, all checked on 21 September 2026. Nothing here rests on it beyond Juslin, Winman and Olsson's account of its argument.

Griffin, D., & Tversky, A. (1992). The weighing of evidence and the determinants of confidence. Cognitive Psychology, 24(3), 411-435. Read in full as the published article, from a copy on a University of Florida course page. The argument this page attributes to them sits on their pages 427 and 428, and was checked there.

Gigerenzer, G., Hoffrage, U., & Kleinbölting, H. (1991). Probabilistic mental models: A Brunswikian theory of confidence. Psychological Review, 98(4), 506-528. Read in full as the published article, from the Max Planck Society's repository. The handle the indexes list is withdrawn, and its replacement's REST bitstream route serves the typeset article, which OpenAlex labels a submitted version. Their finding that judges guess their own percentage correct well was checked in their own text, not only in Merkle.

Brenner, L. (2000). Should observed overconfidence be dismissed as a statistical artifact? Critique of Erev, Wallsten, and Budescu (1994). Psychological Review, 107(4), 943-946. Read in full from the author's own faculty page at the University of Florida. The file is a scan with no text layer, so it was read through optical character recognition, page by page.
